Welcome to the Soccer Year

… To the Players

This handbook will serve as our reference guide for all team principles, team language and more. It is the responsibility of the players to know the language and ultimately apply the concepts! Imagine this as ‘Soccer School’! Ask questions, get answers, be informed!

… To the Parents

As much as we would like the players to apply these principles, we want you to be informed as well! As you go through this document, all of our TEAM TERMINOLOGY will be all the players know. If you are unfamiliar with it, please try to become familiar with it! While we know that everyone wants the best for the athletes, we want to make the learning process simplified by having a terminology everyone understands (i.e. – Shoot it vs. Finish vs. BIG SOCCER KICKS, Susie!).

THE ASK

Speak. Their. Language!

Team Standards

  • Individual Player Development — technically and tactically sophisticated players; developing the modern player (i.e. attacking backs, GKs as field players first): 1% Growth ‘Per Day’ Mentality
  • Program development
  • Create a soccer lifestyle, combined with a fun atmosphere
  • Provide truthful, objective feedback on a daily / weekly / monthly basis

  • Create a soccer environment that is worthwhile and meaningful

Identity Expectations

  • The program will put the players first — Development standards: team specific technical, tactical, physical and mental standards.
  • The players will put the team first — Team standards: the main standard for players is to sacrifice for the team, to suffer for the team.
  • The teams will put the program first — Playing standards: we will have an identity when we step on the field, from every level of play.
NON-NEGOTIABLE

We teach PRINCIPLES not POSITIONS. No matter where you are on the field — “DO YOUR JOB! KNOW YOUR ROLE(S)”

A Note to Parents on Sideline Coaching

Parents have always been told “NO COACHING FROM THE SIDELINES”. However, if you take the language in this document, take the time to learn and understand it, I WANT you coaching from the sidelines!! To be clear, you are only allowed to repeat the language in this document. If not, sit back and enjoy the game very, very quietly!

Addressing Concerns With the Coach (1 of 2)

With the exception of a situation that a parent / guardian deems of critical nature to the well being of one of our athletes, the athletes must confront the coach before a parent / guardian does.

One of the areas of development of an athlete is ‘Self Advocating’ — and the ability to find meaningful ways to resolve situations face-to-face, or even just get basic answers to basic questions, is rapidly becoming a lost skill! We impose a ‘Player First Model’ which helps them to have a voice in their development.

PARENTS

Parents are encouraged to take part in the discussion as a BYSTANDER.

Addressing Concerns With the Coach (2 of 2)

If added conversations are requested by a parent, we follow 2 steps:

  1. Have we already met with the athlete first? (i.e. – is this a player concern or a parent concern?)
  2. As a coach, I work diligently to provide upfront feedback to athletes. If the concern is raised by the parent away from the team / field, address the concern with the athlete. Often times, the parent concern and the player concern aren’t the same (i.e. – the player knows exactly why they’re not playing / starting!)

Start Here

The Vision

Before we jump into the actual soccer content, I want you to visualize something.

►Style of Play ExplanationWatch this first — it is the picture the words below are describing

A team of athletes that can ‘break any line’ moving forward or sideways, building from the back, frustrating opponents by the speed that we play at. We find RELEASE POINTS constantly to force people to chase. We find ‘A-Pass Moments’ into Seam 3 to force teams to defend us vertically. When it’s not on, we recycle and do it all over again.

Two-touch play all over the field until we get into the attacking third and then the skill and athleticism takes over. We have runners everywhere, overlaps, under laps, runs into Seam 3, if it’s not on to get beyond, ‘B Pass Moments’ into Seam 2 …

Our opponent can’t catch us! Players are looking to their coaches on the sideline for answers and even the coaches don’t have any answers.

THE CHOICE

This is a choice everybody has to make right here; RIGHT NOW. If we want to be the best team in the US, it starts now. A mindset shift. A culture shift. We dedicate ourselves to the details in this document.

Home/Contents/Non-Negotiables

Non-Negotiables

Non-Negotiables — Offensively

  • Nearest three positional players are always close and in support, barring opportunities to score.
  • You can never underestimate the value of a ‘bounce pass’. The ability to find simple options to move defenders — even if you make a pass that gets the ball right back to your own feet and doesn’t go anywhere — it will move defenders.
  • ‘Release Points’ lead to ‘A Pass’ Moments. The ability to switch the point of attack will be a staple in how we move the ball forward.
  • 1st and 2nd runners need to be completely in sync. One will empty space, and one will fill space. “One shows, one goes”.
  • In the defensive half of the field, the game requires tempo. Two touches is the goal; we want to move defenders side to side to open up pathways to go forward. In the attacking half, all bets are off — be creative, tons of running off the ball, lots of opportunity to have fun going forward!
  • Midfield rotation is a must. If you get stuck in your position in any attacking sequence, you are holding the team back.
  • Know your runs in the box — all based on the positioning of the ball at the time of the service.

Original handbook page 10
Home/Contents/Non-Negotiables

Non-Negotiables

Non-Negotiables — Defensively

  • Nearest three positional players are SPRINTING — at all times. When it’s your turn to work, you work. When it’s your turn to rest, you rest. That’s the definition of being a team; you share the physical load.
  • 1st defender role is not to win the ball, rather to steer the play — physically begin to impose yourself in 1v1 situations, but do not dive in. EVER. 2nd and 3rd defenders provide cover to deny vertical passing options.
  • Around our goal box, 11 players are expected to be working tirelessly to simply get in the way, defend shots and defend crosses. SACRIFICE IN THE BOX.
  • Whenever you press, you are knowing what you are taking away behind you. Put attackers or passing lanes in your ‘shadow’ and go press to take away options.
  • Upon winning the ball, your transition to keep the ball tells me everything I need to know as a coach. 1-Touch, 1-Touch to get us out of trouble, then simple passing that buys us the time and energy to get our team shape so we can begin to attack.

Formation & Shape

The 3-5-2 Formation

A formation where the natural strength for the team will be having players positioned in wide areas (7 and 11). It will naturally force opponents to bring defenders forward — leaving our forward isolated 1v1 — or drop attacking players to defend in wide areas, allowing us to ‘build’ and bring more numbers forward.

We will attempt to cover questions like:

  • What does ‘Play Dough Theory’ do to help us build?
  • How does the picture adapt when we defend? How do we get into our ‘Fall In Shape’?
  • How do we get more numbers forward to help us attack and cause problems?
  • How does the formation look when rotations start to happen? Do wide players ALWAYS need to be wide?!

We will talk a great deal this year about ‘Positional Play’ and how simply being in the right position (based on the position(s) of others) will set us up for success.

THE BIG PICTURE

We will attack in 5 channels and defend 3 channels. Bottom line, I have 12 things to coach — although the ‘Teaching’ never ends!

Formation & Shape

Fall In Shape — The Detail

Notice the ‘Fall In Shape’. It all matters in terms of the ‘weak side’ of the formation (in reference to where the ball is). Based on the position of the ball, the center backs will naturally slide into position to defend. Our 6 will drop into the gap opened by the center back and the weak side outside back.

The weak side 8 is ready to drop in to create a back-5 if needed, watching to see if she definitively needs to drop in or if she can hang out in midfield to give us numbers.

The weak side 7 / 11 is prepared to drop in to take the place of the weak side 8.

The end result is us creating a block of 5 backs and 4 midfielders, with a single forward who steers the play as she can.

DISCIPLINE

It’s important to understand that we’re not stepping and chasing. We stay underneath the ball and travel together. They eventually HAVE to come forward, so we keep our shape and our discipline to force the turnover and start the counter attacks as needed.

Formation & Shape

Fall In Shape — Watch & Answer

►Fall In Shape — movement video ►Team clip (Google Drive)

Watch the movements. Rewatch the movements. Understand your role(s). Know that maybe a 9 ends up in midfield somewhere … everyone has to know their roles and responsibilities.

Things to take note of

  • Notice how Seam 2 is closed down. There would be no place for someone to receive a pass comfortably.
  • Notice the weakside back (in this video example, the #3) doesn’t even have to move. Why do you think we allow the holding mid to drop in that specific gap?
  • Notice the weakside of the diamond having to drop in as the outside back in a back 5. Why doesn’t the #3 become the outside back?
  • Notice the 10 dropping in to take the place of the holding midfielder.

The center forward should ‘read the game’ and either take away the center back so they can’t switch the point of attack, or ‘screen’ the opposing 6 to deny entry passes into her.

Formation & Shape

The Concept of ‘Seams’

‘Seams’ are simply spaces between lines that we want to use and expose for our benefit, both in possession and in attack. Understanding each seam matters for terminology purposes when we get into possession.

Seam 3

This is for passes and runs to be made. We find ‘A Pass’ Moments and runs to be dangerous. We want to ALWAYS threaten Seam 3 whenever possible!

Seam 2

Where our 10 will live. Where our 9, 7 and 11 will find their ‘B Pass’ Moments, and where our 8’s will seek space when we’re on the offensive.

Seam 1

This will be the least spoken about seam. But it will be important when our 6 or any of our backs ‘live’ in possession.

Attacking Third

Attacking Third — How We’ll Attack (Outside the Box)

Attack

It should be known that our 7 and 11 will be the primary source of width in the team. This is for a few reasons:

  • Because we play primarily against back-4’s, it causes the outside backs to either stay wide — opening up channels in the half space — or stay central, leaving us in a position to find our 7 / 11’s to create services for chances to get to goal.
  • The running into Seam 3, through Channels 2 or 4, is impossible for the opponent to read if done right! Is it going to be our 7 / 11? Is it going to be an 8 on either side? Is it the 9 or 10? It all starts from a position of width.

Blue example

Blue #7 uses a ‘B Pass Moment’ to find the ball at her feet. In doing so, we’d expect the opposing outside back to come out, leaving a giant gap for someone to run into. If the #9 runs through, it drags a center back out, leaving yet another gap for the #10 to run beyond.

Green example

Green #11 uses a ‘B Pass Moment’ to find the ball at her feet. In doing so, we’d expect the opposing outside back to come out, leaving a giant gap for someone to run into.

FREE RANGE

If the pass arrives at the feet of a 7 / 11 and it’s NOT from the 8, they have free range to run beyond the backs!

7’s and 11’s are also encouraged to see the space in Seam 3, through the half-space channels 2 and 4.

Original handbook page 19
Home/Contents/The 12 Moments

Attacking Third

Attacking Third — How We’ll Attack (Inside the Box)

Attack

This simply comes as a kindergarten-themed number match! Look at where the service could come from, match it to where the run should go. L3 Service = L3 Run, and so on. There will be a theme used in our attacking patterns, which can obviously be applied here:

The most dangerous runs in the game come from the weakside of the field.
Finding space in the box, and the timing to match the run to the service, will take a good attacker and make them ELITE.

This will simply come from studying patterns and then applying patterns in training. It is a non-negotiable that players in the attack must understand their runs and their timing. Without it, we rely on luck or individual brilliance to score goals. Give us an advantage by simply knowing your runs, your placement.

** In the areas that are not deemed serving spaces, we are meant to follow the instruction of either keeping playing soccer, scoring goals, or simple rondos to get us out of trouble.

MINDSET

Don’t train until you get it RIGHT. Train until you CAN’T GET IT WRONG!

Attacking Third

Attacking Third — How We’ll Defend

Defend
HEADS UP

Please pay attention if you’re a 7 or 11!

While in the midfield third the 7 or 11 will drop into midfield, here — when the 9 begins to press — the weak side 7 or 11 will look to hunt out the weak side center back, or even sniff out a pass back to a goalkeeper.

The 9 will need to put the opponent’s 6 in their Cover Shadow to deny that pass, and will press the center back.

Strong side 7 / 11 initially denies vertical passing into the midfield third, but anticipates the whole way that their individual match-up with an outside back becomes the only logical passing option. They have to round their run when they press, to deny vertical passing (again) up the line.

Attacking Third

Attacking Third — How We’ll Transition to Defend

Transition to Defend

This doesn’t need any fancy graphics, simply the right mindset.

  1. Sprint. The nearest three players go into a full sprint, forcing the opponent to play either laterally or backwards. And we mean SPRINT as if your job depended on it! We will be committing so many players forward, we can’t get beat in this moment.
  2. Foul, if you must. If you’re about to get beat individually, you foul. Our nickname for this is either ‘Molly’ or ‘Kill Counter Attacks’.
  3. Recover. If we get beat by direct play or a long ball clearance, we go into RECOVERY RUNNING.

Midfield Third

Midfield Third — How We’ll Attack

Attack

Unless the opportunity presents itself with 100% certainty to go forward, we need to find at least a single RELEASE POINT in the midfield third, to do a couple of things:

  • Lateral passing opens Seam 2 by dragging the 6 out of position.
  • Simple passing draws opponents forward to open Seam 3.

With a well executed Release Point, it will also allow numbers-up situations to go forward and allow for plenty of options to the ball carrier.

If a right or left center back is able to penetrate and join in the midfield, they should. Our movement should drag the opponent back more, which kills counter attacks (i.e. there are fewer players to counter attack with if we get our numbers forward).

Midfield Third

Midfield Third — How We’ll Defend (1 of 2)

Defend
  • 9 — Forces play into wide areas (doesn’t chase center back(s)). Rounds run to deny pass back to center back.
  • 7 — Gets underneath the outside back to deny vertical passing into the wide forward.
  • 11 (weakside) — Rotates into midfield to pick up the weakside attacking midfielder.
  • 10 — Slides into the pocket where they could pick off either the 6 or the nearside attacking midfielder.
  • 8 (nearside) — Slides into position to deny pass into their 9.
  • 8 (weakside) — Drops inline vertically with outside center back, READY to drop into a wingback role if needed.
  • 6 — Slides across to help deny vertical pass into the 9.
  • Outside center back (nearside) — Slides across to go man-to-man with the wide forward.
  • Center back and weakside center back — Slide across to create a 2v1 against the target center forward.

Midfield Third

Midfield Third — How We’ll Transition to Attack

Transition to Attack

Change. Your. Zone.

Because we “defend in 3 zones”, our transition to attack has to stretch and get us into our “attacking in 5 zones” faster than the opponent can transition to press us and win the ball back.

Notice the greyed-out starting positions (defensive shape in 3 zones) versus the blue attacking shape (attacking in 5 zones).

But back to basics … once we win possession back:

  • Closest 3 to the ball, SUPPORT (ideally changing zones). Now we ‘rondo our way out of trouble’.
  • The rest STRETCH to give us Release Points.

Midfield Third

Midfield Third — How We’ll Transition to Defend

Transition to Defend
PRIORITY #1

This is THE MOST IMPORTANT MOMENT of the 12 moments we are trying to define here.

This moment is nothing more than effort:

  • Closest 3 players hunt (defensively) like rabid animals. And I mean RABID. Crazy effort!
  • While the closest 3 hunt, everyone else falls into line to prevent entry into our defensive third.
  • Positioning to deny entry into our defensive third is paramount. Get where you need to be … DO YOUR JOB!

Defensive Third

Defensive Third — How We’ll Attack

Attack

While this is the ‘defensive third’, it extends through our entire half, to better understand how we’re going to ‘build’.

►Building Out of the BackVideo from the original handbook contents page

The basic setup is simple. Get the wide parts of the diamond as wide as can be to drag the midfielders away. Set up with our back three and holding midfield players to create a 5v3 in and around the goal box. The front three stay up at midfield to ‘pin’ the back 4 of the opposition. The #10 has to commit their #6 to marking, not pressing.

Seam 1

Space between the opposing forward line and midfield line.

Seam 2

Space between the midfield line and the back 4.

Seam 3

Space beyond the back 4.

It’s also important to understand A-Pass Moments and Release Points to make sure that the information here makes sense. Until you understand our team language, the following phrase will sound foreign:

Entry passes into Seam 1, then finding release points that lead to A-Pass Moments into Seam 3; ‘1 shows, 1 goes’, rotating through late runners into the most dangerous runners (weakside runners) into dangerous scoring positions to find attempts on goal.

There is another language we’re learning. Please understand this comes through repetition and asking questions to gain understanding where the athletes currently don’t understand. Goal kicks can lead to breakaways if we’re smart!

Defensive Third

Defensive Third — How We’ll Defend

Defend
  • You’ll notice the holding mid drops into the weakside gap between center back and R/L center back, allowing the weakside center back to retain marking vs. the weakside opponent — creating a back 4.
  • Remaining 3 in midfield ‘flatten out’ into a block of 3 above the back 4.
  • Weakside forward drops in to SPLIT THE DIFFERENCE between helping defend in midfield vs. dealing with a switch of play.
  • The center forward (#9) will get to the side of the nearest opponent center back to take away the switch.
  • The weakside part of the diamond (the #6 here) gets to the nearside of the opposing attacking central midfielder. The nearside of our diamond (#8 here) tracks runners, if there are any.
  • We. Hunt. And hunt. And hunt! There is maximum effort here; sprinting by the closest 3 players to the ball while the remaining 7 field players are SO over-the-top bought in to their positioning and their marks. We fight and make any attempt forward a struggle.
  • The GK’s ‘Vision Spot’ is a constant check. Quick scans while you communicate to weakside teammates to make sure they’re where you NEED them to be. Not where you WANT them to be! (Big difference!)

Refer to Fall In Shape.

The goal of defending the final third is not counter attacking. The goal is to keep the opponent out of the goal. We defend here with all 11.

Defensive Third

Defensive Third — How We’ll Transition to Attack

Transition to Attack

When we win possession …

If we can win possession cleanly, recognizing numbers should allow us a small rondo to find our way out of trouble. Utilizing principles like 1-Touch, 1-Touch, this rondo will give us a small bit of quick possession to establish a tempo that will eventually help us out to our (yellow) supporting players in the next image …

The goal of the transition …

Through our (yellow) supporting players, the closest to the ball (#8 here) is our ‘Spare Player’ in the rondo. Spare players change quickly, but finding the spare player can help us find our Release Points. If not, the supporting center back (#4 here) dropping into a pocket with an eye out for our release points will allow us the opportunity to find an attack quickly out of nowhere.

Defensive Third

Defensive Third — How We’ll Transition to Defend

Transition to Defend

RED — Urgency to press

The nearest 3 defenders underneath / closest to the ball HUNT. Like crazy animals. Go force bad decisions through pressure and deny early service / finishing attempts to be a danger to our goal. The #9 becomes MASSIVE here, getting tight to the nearside center back (in this example) to deny the switch.

YELLOW — Urgency for positional shape

The ‘Spine’ of the team finds their way into their tactical positions to make sure we’re set up to defend. (See Defending in the Final Third.)

GREEN — Positional (‘What’s my role?’)

The farthest few players from the position of the ball. These players are both sliding into position and picking up marks to make sure the team has its shape. Their biggest role is their VOICE and their ORGANIZATION, to make sure those closer to the ball are in a position to keep the opponent away from goal.

** If we’ve lost possession outside the final third, now it becomes about RECOVERY RUNNING and getting everybody behind the ball. **

Team Language

Goalkeeper Principles

Communicate and Organize

Because there won’t be any actual ‘defending’ from a goalkeeper, their job on the defensive side of the team comes down to 2 items: communicate with and organize your defenders.

Don’t overcorrect our shape — know what our Fall In Shape should look like for each player in the team.

REMEMBER

There is no more important voice than the goalkeeper.

Team Language

Defensive Terminology (1 of 2)

As a Group See it →

Close space together — can we press together as a unit?

Back Line is Too High / Press / Squeeze

Back line needs to drop and tuck in, or do something together as a unit.

Get Tight / Close Down (Don’t Foul)

Do not let the attacker turn, or apply immediate pressure. That doesn’t mean run someone over!

Press Together (6 Second Press) See it →

The act of pressing the ball all together, abandoning positions at times, to throw all numbers at winning possession back as quickly as possible. No positions, just effort. THIS IS A 100% SPRINT BY ALL.

Make It Difficult

When there is a bad pass, bad touch, or the ball is bouncing — fight for every opportunity to cause ‘chaos’ in helping to win possession back, or cause a turnover.

Take Away the Next One See it →

Use your vision to take away the next, easiest passing option. Could be a person to go defend, or it could be a gap to step into so they can’t pass through that gap.

Press Together has two deep-dive pages: Page 1 — why 6 seconds · Page 2 — what it looks like

Original handbook page 35
Home/Contents/Team Language

Team Language

Defensive Terminology (2 of 2)

Check Shoulders / Rule of 3 Flags See it →

Using a little geometry, this refers to your arms making a 160 degree angle, with 1 hand pointing towards the ball and the other hand at your mark (gap to defend, etc).

Split the Difference See it →

Don’t defend any 1 player or gap — instead, sit in between 2 defensive points to be able to get to EITHER. Thus, you’re splitting your interests to defend twice as much!

Kill the Counter (‘Molly’)

If need be, use a soft foul on purpose to slow a counter attack. Will only be seen on our offensive corner kicks / set pieces, deep possession.

Recovery Runs See it →

If the ball has passed you, your ability to get back behind the ball and help us get numbers up.

Recover, Regroup and Repress

When an individual is beaten by a pass or a run: RECOVER to the mass of defenders, REGROUP collectively on what everyone’s new roles are, and then REPRESS — which should be self-explanatory!

Team Language

Attacking Terminology (1 of 2)

Entry Pass See it →

Find targets or a pass through a gap into the next ‘line’ of the team. Break lines with passing.

Team Language

Attacking Terminology (2 of 2)

Change Your Running / Runs See it →

If the 1st run you’ve made was not successful, the requirement is that you simply change your running in a different direction or at a different angle. It’s a must.

This Side is Closed See it →

Also heard as ‘change the point of attack’. Get the ball off the side of the field it’s currently on, to try and attack the open side of the field.

Get Into the Gaps See it →

Finding space in an opposition’s defense. Find a pair of defending players (anywhere on the field) and sit behind the imaginary line the 2 players are connected by.

Team Language

Counter Terminology

1 Touch, 1 Touch See it →

Used when starting a counter attack. Get the first available touch away ASAP, followed by a 2nd 1-touch pass to clear defensive pressure.

‘A’ Pass Moments / ‘B’ Pass Moments See it →

In anticipation of winning possession back, how early can we start offensive movement and find ‘A’ pass moments (passes that get behind the back 4) or ‘B’ pass moments (in front)? Also: start your runs early.

Play Dough Theory See it →

Ever hold play dough in your hand and use your other hand to squish it out? The idea of ‘compressing space’ and forcing a reaction out of the play dough to have to ‘squish’ out of your hand. This theory relates to principles in possession which will help with RELEASE POINTS.

Release Points See it →

Find a ‘weak side’ player (who is finding space of their own) to break pressure and attack the opposite side of the field. Used with ‘This Side is Closed’.

Defending, in Detail

Pressing — The 6 Seconds

The commonly known phrase of the “Barcelona 6-second press” was made famous in modern football by Pep Guardiola, utilizing the notion that it takes on average 7–8 seconds for a team to get into their full attacking shape when they’ve won possession. So, naturally, if you can win the ball back in 6 seconds, you’ve beaten the opponent in a small, but critical area.

Work 10% harder on defense, enjoy 10% more possession of the ball.

This quote, when given analysis at top levels of our game, refers to roughly 9 minutes more possession (90 minute game) and approximately ¾ to 1 mile less running without the ball — because your team has possession. That’s a lot!

Defending, in Detail

Press Together (6 Second Press)

This process is an immediate reaction to when we lose possession. How quickly can we get the full 10 field players into a quadrant of the field to defend, take away all gaps / options, and force them back into a turnover for us to try to score?

Combine with 1-touch, 1-touch to get us out of trouble and begin to keep the ball away from the opponent.

WHY 6?

Why 6 seconds? Because the average for a team to get into their attacking shape is 7 seconds. Win the ball back before a team can get into their team shape.

Defending, in Detail

Take Away the Next One — A vs. B

When you ‘Take Away the Next One’, it refers to a mentality of making educated guesses on what your opponent is going to do next with the ball.

Scenario A

Assuming that defensively, the pass is going to be played directly to a person. So ‘taking away the next player’ is the option that appears to be the most dangerous to our team.

Scenario B

Assuming that defensively, the pass is going to be played into a space. Therefore, defensively, players are moving into gaps that they are assuming the passes are going to be played into.

Attacking, in Detail

1-Touch, 1-Touch

A concept that nobody else works on in transition moments, to begin to pull the ball out of pressure through 2 consecutive 1-touch passes. The reason this becomes effective is: when an attacker loses the ball, they are taught to immediately win the ball back. There is no faster way to get the ball out of pressure than with a single 1-touch!

Now, as the previous attacker chases down the 1st touch we’ve just used to get out of pressure, a quick 2nd 1-touch pass will force nearly every pressing player to just give up. Maybe it’s too far a run? Maybe they’re just frustrated? Maybe in a play and get it back scenario, they just don’t have the energy to continue pressing!

Attacking, in Detail

‘A’ Pass / ‘B’ Pass Moments

This should be simple: A comes before B.

We want to go to ‘A’ areas first if the option is available, noticing IF space is there to run into — i.e. an ‘A’ Pass Moment, or get behind the backs of the opponent.

‘B’ comes second, as if it’s considered a lesser option — but one that should be explored to keep possession when needed. SEAM 3 becomes the term we will refer to here.

Attacking, in Detail

Release Points

As if we were splitting the field in half (vertically), the phrase ‘Release Points’ has meaning for both the person with the ball, as well as those who have the potential to become the release point.

  • The player with the ball is reminded that THIS SIDE IS CLOSED and should look to RELEASE pressure through lateral passing.
  • The players without the ball are reminded to get to the opposite side of the imaginary line, to help us expand the field.

Release Points lead to ‘A’ Pass Moments.

Attacking Set Pieces

What is an Indirect Free Kick?

Unlike a direct free kick, a goal may not be scored directly from the kick; the ball must first come into contact with another player (from either team). If the ball goes into the goal without touching any other player, a goal kick is awarded. The law was derived from the Sheffield Rules, which stated that no goal could be scored from a free kick.

An indirect free kick is awarded to the opposing team when a player infringes certain technical requirements of the laws (e.g. touching the ball a second time following a restart, or the keeper touching the ball with their hands when a teammate has used their foot to pass it back). An indirect free kick is also awarded when play is stopped to caution or send off a player when no specific foul has occurred (e.g. when play is stopped to caution a player for dissenting the decision of the referee).

The most common cause is the offside offence, and it is notated by a referee’s arm being held vertically until both the free kick has been taken and subsequently touched a 2nd time by any player.

IN THE BOX

Unlike a direct free kick, an offence inside the goal box will not result in a penalty; rather, it continues to be taken as an indirect free kick.

NON-NEGOTIABLE

We defend corners with all 11.

The nearest matching number of players will confront the corner, with the team shape simply falling in to create stability in dangerous areas.

Defensive Set Pieces

Bullet (Wo)Man

Sending a bullet-man to block indirect free kicks is simple. A bullet-man lines up as an extended part of the wall, leaving a 1-person gap on the interior of the wall (inside the goal frame) to explode like a bullet — or a track star ‘off the blocks’ — to sacrifice themselves by obstructing the shooter.

The bullet-man leaves to defend the second the ball is put in play by the person starting the indirect set piece.

CRITICAL

They attack the BALL, not a player.

Original handbook page 73
Home/Contents/Set Pieces

Defensive Set Pieces

Setting Walls for Goalkeepers (1 of 3)

  1. The goalkeeper is in control. They dictate everything, from the number in the wall to how far the wall shifts based on what they see.
  2. The player on the interior of the wall is turned to take instruction from the GK.
  3. BIG arm movements point in the direction to move the wall. NOT ‘right’ and ‘left’ — because for the person facing you, their right and left is different. Point in the direction you want (“2 steps this way”, or “½ a step this way”).
THE RULE

When setting the wall, there must be 1 player OUTSIDE the direct line from the ball to the post. The player on the outside of this line must be the TALLEST person standing in the wall.

Notice that the inside player is facing the goalkeeper, taking direction and pushing / pulling the wall where they need to go. Everyone in the wall is locked arms!

Defensive Set Pieces

Setting Walls for Goalkeepers (2 of 3)

Immediately following a foul against us with the opponent in a shooting situation, someone immediately needs to confront the ball to deny the early shot before we are set.

If you get put into the wall, everyone is locked arms, and the player on the inside of the wall is turned to face the GK to receive direction on wall placement.

That same player — we’ll call them the ‘Wall Captain’ — gets everyone to jump at the time of the shot against us. When you jump, you must point your toes so a ball doesn’t get underneath the wall being set. It makes you as tall as you can be!

Quick Reference

Numbers & Roles — Quick Reference

New in this guide

This page isn’t in the original handbook — it’s a cheat sheet built from it, so you can decode the numbers used on every other page.

1

Goalkeeper

Communicate and organize. The ‘Vision Spot’ is a constant check.GK Principles →

2 / 3

Outside backs / wide defenders

On defensive corners, 2 and 3 mark the goal posts. The weakside back holds position in Fall In Shape.

4 / 5

Center backs (R / L center back)

Slide across to create a 2v1 on the target forward. If they can penetrate and join midfield, they should.

6

Holding midfielder

Drops into the gap opened by the center back and weakside outside back. Drives Play Dough Theory.

8

Central midfielders (the diamond)

Nearside denies the pass into their 9; weakside drops in line, ready for a wingback role.

10

Attacking midfielder

Lives in Seam 2. Slides into the pocket to pick off the 6 or the nearside attacking mid. On defensive corners, attacks the service wherever it goes.

7 / 11

Wide forwards

Our primary source of width. Drop into midfield in the middle third; hunt the weakside center back in the attacking third.

9

Center forward

Forces play wide, rounds runs, puts the opposing 6 in their cover shadow. Massive in transition to defend.

ASK YOUR COACH

One thing to confirm with your coach: the handbook refers to the holding midfielder as the #6 in most places, but as the #5 on the Defensive Third — Defend page. Same role, and the diagrams make it clear — just ask so nobody is guessing.

Quick Reference

Glossary (A–Z)

New in this guide

Every term in the handbook, in one A–Z list. Tap any term to jump straight to the page that explains it. Use the search box up top if you would rather type it.

1st Runners, 2nd RunnersA reminder for players in an area of possession to find the beginning stages of their movement, followed by those ‘running off’ each other to start their runs next.1 Touch, 1 TouchUsed when starting a counter attack. Get the first available touch away ASAP, followed by a 2nd 1-touch pass to clear defensive pressure.‘A’ Pass Moments / ‘B’ Pass MomentsIn anticipation of winning possession back, how early can we start offensive movement and find ‘A’ pass moments (passes that get behind the back 4) or ‘B’ pass moments (in front)? Also: start your runs early.As a GroupClose space together — can we press together as a unit?Back Line is Too High / Press / SqueezeBack line needs to drop and tuck in, or do something together as a unit.Change Your Running / RunsIf the 1st run you’ve made was not successful, the requirement is that you simply change your running in a different direction or at a different angle. It’s a must.Check Shoulders / Rule of 3 FlagsUsing a little geometry, this refers to your arms making a 160 degree angle, with 1 hand pointing towards the ball and the other hand at your mark (gap to defend, etc).Entry PassFind targets or a pass through a gap into the next ‘line’ of the team. Break lines with passing.‘Get At Him / Her’, ‘Go 1 on 1’Run at the space / defender with the ball.Get Into the GapsFinding space in an opposition’s defense. Find a pair of defending players (anywhere on the field) and sit behind the imaginary line the 2 players are connected by.Get Tight / Close Down (Don’t Foul)Do not let the attacker turn, or apply immediate pressure. That doesn’t mean run someone over!Kill the Counter (‘Molly’)If need be, use a soft foul on purpose to slow a counter attack. Will only be seen on our offensive corner kicks / set pieces, deep possession.Make It DifficultWhen there is a bad pass, bad touch, or the ball is bouncing — fight for every opportunity to cause ‘chaos’ in helping to win possession back, or cause a turnover.Play and Get It BackMake a simple pass, then become an immediate option again.Play and Join / Break Lines With Your RunsPlay the ball forward and get forward to support. Use your running to get to the next line.Play Dough TheoryEver hold play dough in your hand and use your other hand to squish it out? The idea of ‘compressing space’ and forcing a reaction out of the play dough to have to ‘squish’ out of your hand. This theory relates to principles in possession which will help with RELEASE POINTS.Press Together (6 Second Press)The act of pressing the ball all together, abandoning positions at times, to throw all numbers at winning possession back as quickly as possible. No positions, just effort. THIS IS A 100% SPRINT BY ALL.Recover, Regroup and RepressWhen an individual is beaten by a pass or a run: RECOVER to the mass of defenders, REGROUP collectively on what everyone’s new roles are, and then REPRESS — which should be self-explanatory!Recovery RunsIf the ball has passed you, your ability to get back behind the ball and help us get numbers up.Release PointsFind a ‘weak side’ player (who is finding space of their own) to break pressure and attack the opposite side of the field. Used with ‘This Side is Closed’.Split the DifferenceDon’t defend any 1 player or gap — instead, sit in between 2 defensive points to be able to get to EITHER. Thus, you’re splitting your interests to defend twice as much!Take Away the Next OneUse your vision to take away the next, easiest passing option. Could be a person to go defend, or it could be a gap to step into so they can’t pass through that gap.This Side is ClosedAlso heard as ‘change the point of attack’. Get the ball off the side of the field it’s currently on, to try and attack the open side of the field.
